title: Units, division rings, fields, and finite domains
terms: unit; division ring; field; subfield; finite field; quadratic field; quaternion division ring; strictly skew field.

exposition.text:
A unit has a two-sided multiplicative inverse. A division ring is a nonzero unital ring in which
every nonzero element is a unit; a field is a commutative division ring. Every field is a domain,
but Z is a domain that is not a field. Every finite domain is a field because multiplication by a
nonzero element is injective and therefore surjective on a finite set.

question.text:
Let R be a finite commutative ring with identity and no nonzero zero divisors. If R has 49
elements, how many units does it contain?
(A) 6 (B) 7 (C) 42 (D) 48 (E) 49

solution.text:
A finite integral domain is a field: for a ̸= 0, the map x 7→ ax is injective, hence hits 1.
Thus exactly the 49 − 1 = 48 nonzero elements are units.

question.text:
In the real quaternions, let q, r satisfy (1 + i)q = j and r(1 + i) = j. Which pair (q, r) is correct?
(A) ((j − k)/2, (j + k)/2) (B) ((j + k)/2, (j − k)/2)
(C) ((j − k)/2, (j − k)/2) (D) (j − k, j + k)
(E) ((j + k)/2, (j + k)/2)

solution.text:
The inverse of 1 + i is (1 − i)/2. Multiplying the first equation on the left gives q = (1 −
i)j/2 = (j − k)/2. Multiplying the second on the right gives r = j(1 − i)/2 = (j + k)/2, since
ij = k but ji = −k. The side on which one divides matters.

question.text:
How many units does Z × Z × F have?
12 4
(A) 12 (B) 16 (C) 24 (D) 32 (E) 48

solution.text:
A tuple is invertible exactly when every coordinate is invertible, with coordinatewise in-
verse. The three factors have 2, φ(12) = 4, and 4−1 = 3 units. Thus the count is 2·4·3 = 24.
The zero coordinate in a field is not allowed.
